1. Project Overview

Diabetes is one of the leading chronic diseases globally. This project builds a supervised binary classification system that predicts whether a person is at risk of diabetes based on 21 health and lifestyle indicators from the US CDC.

Primary Goals High recall — catch as many diabetic patients as possible | Model transparency via SHAP — explain every prediction | Practical deployment via Streamlit web app
Why recall matters more than accuracy Missing a diabetic patient (false negative) is clinically more costly than a false alarm. A false alarm leads to unnecessary follow-up. A missed diagnosis leads to untreated disease. All design decisions — SMOTE, threshold optimisation, metric choice — reflect this.

2. Dataset Description

CDC Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) 2015
Source: Kaggle — Alex Teboul

The BRFSS is an annual telephone survey conducted by the CDC across all 50 US states, collecting health behaviour data from over 400,000 adults per year.

4. Data Preprocessing

Split Strategy: 80 / 5 / 15

SetSizeRowsClass BalancePurpose
Training80%~202,905 → 349,268 after SMOTE50/50 (after SMOTE)Model training
Validation5%~12,72386/14 (real)Threshold search only
Test15%~38,05286/14 (real)Final evaluation
Critical design decision Validation and test sets are split before SMOTE, preserving real 86/14 class distribution. This ensures threshold search and final evaluation happen on realistic data.

SMOTE — Training Only

from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
sm = SMOTE(random_state=42)
X_train, y_train = sm.fit_resample(X_trainval, y_trainval)
# Before: [174,634 non-diabetic, 28,271 diabetic]
# After : [174,634 non-diabetic, 174,634 diabetic]  ← balanced

StandardScaler

scaler         = StandardScaler()
X_train_sc     = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)   # fit + transform
X_val_sc       = scaler.transform(X_val)          # transform only
X_test_sc      = scaler.transform(X_test)         # transform only
# Tree models (RF, XGBoost, LightGBM) use RAW data — scale-invariant

5. Feature Engineering

Three clinically-motivated composite features added on top of the original 21:

MetabolicRisk

BMI×0.4 + HighBP×10 + HighChol×8 + HeartDisease×12 + Stroke×10

Combines the 5 strongest cardiometabolic risk factors. Ranked 3rd globally in SHAP (Mean |SHAP|=0.378) — above individual features like BMI and HighBP.

LifestyleScore

PhysActivity×3 + Fruits + Veggies - Smoker×2 - HvyAlcohol×2

Healthy lifestyle proxy. Physical activity weighted ×3 (strongest evidence-based intervention). Smoking and heavy alcohol reduce the score.

HealthcareBurden

MentHlth + PhysHlth

Total days of poor health in past 30 days. Captures chronic illness burden which correlates strongly with diabetes progression.

7. Hyperparameter Tuning

Method: RandomizedSearchCV 40 random combinations × 5-fold stratified CV. Scoring metric: F1 (not accuracy). All CPU cores used (n_jobs=-1). Tuning on 60,000-row sample for speed, full retrain after.

Best Parameters — XGBoost (CV F1 = 0.9129)

learning_rate=0.08, max_depth=7, subsample=0.6,
colsample_bytree=0.7, gamma=0.1, reg_alpha=0.5,
reg_lambda=0.5, min_child_weight=3, n_estimators=200

Best Parameters — LightGBM (CV F1 = 0.9140)

learning_rate=0.08, num_leaves=127, max_depth=4,
subsample=0.9, colsample_bytree=0.6, reg_alpha=0.1,
reg_lambda=1.0, min_child_samples=10, n_estimators=500,
class_weight='balanced'
Note on CV F1 = 0.91 This is computed on SMOTE-balanced training folds. Test-set F1 at default threshold is lower (~0.27) because the class distribution returns to real 86/14 — this is expected and correct. ROC-AUC 0.971 is the meaningful number.

8. Model Evaluation Strategy

MetricFormulaWhy Used
ROC-AUC ★Area under ROC curvePrimary. Threshold-independent, robust to imbalance
F1-Score2×P×R/(P+R)Balances precision and recall at chosen threshold
Recall (Sensitivity)TP/(TP+FN)% of diabetics correctly identified — most clinically important
PrecisionTP/(TP+FP)% of predicted diabetics actually diabetic
Accuracy(TP+TN)/TotalReported only — misleading with 86/14 imbalance
Why accuracy is misleading here A model predicting "No Diabetes" always: Accuracy = 86.1% ✓ | Recall = 0% ✗ | ROC-AUC = 0.5 ✗ ROC-AUC correctly identifies this as a random classifier.

9. Threshold Optimisation

At default threshold 0.50, XGBoost: Accuracy=86.4% but Recall=19% — misses 81% of diabetics.

precisions, recalls, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_val, probs)
f1_scores    = 2 * precisions * recalls / (precisions + recalls)
best_thresh  = thresholds[np.argmax(f1_scores)]
Key design: search on real-distribution validation set The validation set is split before SMOTE (86/14 distribution = same as deployment). If we searched on SMOTE-balanced data, the optimal threshold (~0.50) would be wrong.

10. SHAP Explainability

SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) assigns each feature a contribution score for every prediction, based on game theory's Shapley values.

Key Properties Locally accurate (SHAP values sum to prediction) | Consistent (higher importance → higher SHAP) | TreeExplainer is exact and fast for tree models

Top 10 Features — Tuned XGBoost

1. GenHlth (General Health)0.766
2. Age0.451
3. MetabolicRisk (engineered)0.378
4. BMI0.309
5. Education0.209
6. Sex0.184
7. HighBP0.183
8. Income0.176
9. Fruits0.129
10. DiffWalk0.118
Validation of feature engineering MetabolicRisk (engineered) ranks 3rd globally — above individual features BMI (4th) and HighBP (7th). This confirms the composite feature carries real, non-redundant signal.

PatternDiagnosisFix
Large train-val gapOverfittingRegularise, reduce complexity
Both curves low & convergedUnderfittingMore features, complex model
Val curve still risingMore data would helpCollect more data
Val curve plateaued, small gapWell-fitted ✓—

Observations: XGBoost/LightGBM show small train-val gap — well-fitted. Logistic Regression converges early — bias-limited (non-linear data). Random Forest shows slight gap — variance present but reduces with more data.

13. Interview Preparation

60-Second Pitch "I built an end-to-end diabetes risk prediction system using 253,680 real CDC survey records — not the standard PIMA dataset. I trained 8 models including tuned XGBoost and LightGBM with RandomizedSearchCV, handled class imbalance with SMOTE on training data only, and added SHAP explainability. The best model achieves ROC-AUC 0.826 on the real 86/14 test set. I engineered a MetabolicRisk feature that ranked 3rd in SHAP — above individual features like blood pressure and cholesterol. Deployed as a 4-tab Streamlit web app."

Level 1 — Basics

Basic What problem does this project solve?
Early detection of diabetes risk from health and lifestyle survey data. The model flags high-risk individuals for medical screening, enabling preventive intervention before clinical diagnosis.
Basic Why CDC BRFSS instead of PIMA Indians dataset?
PIMA has only 768 rows from one specific ethnic group. CDC BRFSS has 253,680 real records from a diverse US adult population across all 50 states. It's more realistic, generalisable, and cited in peer-reviewed papers in Nature and NIH journals (2024–2025).
Basic What accuracy did you get?
Accuracy is misleading here — with 86% non-diabetic, any model always predicting "No Diabetes" gets 86%. I report ROC-AUC (0.826) and F1 (0.466). The model correctly identifies 61.7% of diabetic patients (recall), which is the clinically meaningful number.

Level 2 — Technical

Technical What is SMOTE and why training data only?
SMOTE creates synthetic minority-class samples by interpolating between existing ones in feature space. Applied only to training data because validation and test sets must represent real class distribution (86/14). Applying to test data would create artificially optimistic results — data leakage.
Technical Explain your train/val/test split design.
80% training (SMOTE-balanced to 50/50) | 5% validation — pre-SMOTE, real 86/14 — used only for threshold search | 15% test — pre-SMOTE, real 86/14 — held out until final evaluation. The critical decision: validation split before SMOTE ensures threshold search at real distribution.
Technical Why threshold = 0.24 instead of 0.5?
At 0.5 threshold, XGBoost recall = 19% (misses 81% of diabetics). SMOTE training teaches 50/50 balance, but test time returns to 86/14 — models assign low probabilities to positive. Lowering threshold to 0.24 trades precision for recall, raising F1 from 0.279 to 0.465 and recall from 19% to 65%.
Technical What is the bias-variance tradeoff and where does it appear?
Bias = error from oversimplified assumptions (underfitting). Variance = sensitivity to training data (overfitting). Logistic Regression has high bias on this non-linear data. Deep Random Forest shows variance — training-validation gap in learning curves. XGBoost's gamma, reg_alpha, reg_lambda control this tradeoff, explaining why tuning improved it.
Technical Gini importance vs SHAP — what's the difference?
Gini importance measures impurity reduction across all trees — biased toward high-cardinality features, doesn't capture interactions. SHAP computes exact Shapley values — model-agnostic, locally accurate (sum to prediction), no cardinality bias. GenHlth ranks first in both, confirming consistency. SHAP additionally shows direction and magnitude per sample.

Level 3 — Advanced

Advanced How does XGBoost work mathematically?
XGBoost builds trees sequentially fitting the negative gradient of the loss function (gradient descent in function space). Objective: L = Σ l(ŷᵢ, yᵢ) + Σ Ω(fₖ) where Ω = γT + ½λ||w||² (T=leaves, w=leaf weights). Uses second-order Taylor approximation for efficient closed-form leaf weight computation.
Advanced Give 3 ways you prevented data leakage.
(1) StandardScaler fit only on training data — prevents test statistics influencing normalisation. (2) SMOTE applied only to training data — prevents synthetic test samples. (3) Threshold optimisation on held-out validation set, never the test set — prevents threshold overfitting.
Advanced Why did the Stacking Ensemble underperform?
Two reasons: (1) All base learners (RF, XGBoost, LightGBM) are tree-based — correlated, make similar errors on same samples. True stacking needs architecturally diverse base models. (2) Base learners trained on SMOTE-balanced data produce probability scales that don't align with the real-distribution meta-learner evaluation. Platt scaling / isotonic regression would fix this.
Advanced What would you do next to improve this?
(1) Optuna for Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation. (2) Platt scaling for probability calibration. (3) Feature selection with RFE to reduce noise. (4) Temporal validation — train on BRFSS 2014/2015, test on 2016/2017. (5) TabNet or simple MLP for neural network comparison.

Resume Bullet Points

• Built end-to-end diabetes risk prediction system on 253,680 CDC BRFSS records
  using XGBoost, LightGBM, and Stacking Ensemble; achieved ROC-AUC 0.826

• Applied SMOTE (training only), RandomizedSearchCV (40×5-fold, CV F1=0.913/0.914),
  threshold optimisation raising XGBoost F1 from 0.279 → 0.465

• Engineered 3 composite features (MetabolicRisk, LifestyleScore, HealthcareBurden);
  MetabolicRisk ranked 3rd globally by SHAP feature importance

• Implemented SHAP explainability (global summary + per-patient waterfall plots)
  and deployed as 4-tab Streamlit web app

14. How to Run

1. Install dependencies

pip install -r requirements.txt

2. Download dataset

# Go to:
# https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/alexteboul/diabetes-health-indicators-dataset
# Download and place in data/ folder

3. Run full pipeline (~25–30 min)

python run_pipeline.py

4. Launch web app

python -m streamlit run app/streamlit_app.py
# Open: http://localhost:8501

15. Limitations & Future Work

Current Limitations

LimitationDetail
Self-reported dataBRFSS telephone survey — responses may not be medically accurate
No clinical measurementsNo blood glucose, HbA1c, insulin — the most direct indicators
Cross-sectionalOne point in time — cannot capture disease progression
US population onlyMay not generalise to other countries or ethnic groups
Stacking EnsembleNeeded manual threshold fix — probability recalibration required
Moderate F1 (~0.47)Real limitation of survey features vs clinical measurements

Future Work

  1. Optuna — Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation (more efficient than RandomizedSearchCV)
  2. Probability Calibration — Platt scaling / isotonic regression for reliable probability estimates
  3. Temporal Validation — Train on 2014/2015, test on 2016/2017 BRFSS
  4. Multi-class — Extend to 3-class using diabetes_012 file
  5. Neural Network — TabNet or MLP comparison baseline
  6. Cloud Deployment — Deploy on Streamlit Community Cloud or Hugging Face Spaces
